A spatial lag model (SLM) can be estimated in R using the command `lagsarlm()`, which is in the **spatialreg** package. Lagrange Multiplier (LM) is a test for the absence of spatial autocorrelation in the lag model residuals. results.title: What Is Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR)? - GIS Geography
results.content: *Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) is a spatial statistical technique that models the relationship between a dependent variable and independent variables while allowing for spatial variation in the model parameters, making it sensitive to local geographic variations.*. Spatial regression models are also used to predict future crime locations and even in other cities. Let’s use spatial regression to model spatial relationships between marsh deer and land features. When the OLS regression models tools give the WARNING 000851 at the end of the report, this means that the Spatial Autocorrelation (Moran’s I) Tool should be processed to ensure residuals are not spatially autocorrelated. We built a spatial relationship between Marsh deer, campgrounds, roads, and wetlands using the spatial regression tool. The variance inflation factor, z-scores, Jarque-Bera, and Moran’s I ensured robustness and statistical significance in the spatial regression model. The regression model shows how Marsh deer select wetlands as a suitable habitat. The regression model can also predict Marsh deer in other areas.

results.title: Spatial Regression - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
results.content: Spatial regression is defined as a statistical technique used to model and analyze the relationship between a dependent variable, such as the incidence of dermatologic diseases, and independent variables while accounting for spatial autocorrelation among observations. It addresses the violation of the independence of errors assumption common in traditional regression models by incorporating spatial dependencies in the analysis. ### R7: Increasing Use of Spatial Regression Modeling Approaches. With an increasing volume of GIS data and RS images, they should be utilized more in obesity research, such as geographically (and temporally) weighted regression, spatial lag models, and spatial error models [4]. Conventional and spatial statistical methods should be used in conjunction, such as spatial multilevel modeling, to explore spatially varying effects of environmental variables on obesogenic behaviors and obesity [68]. Spatial regression specifications are most useful to researchers seeking to either investigate a spatialized version of a dependent or independent variable, or account for spatial autocorrelation observed in data that would violate traditional regression assumptions (Anselin, 2011). A few studies combined SLM and SEM models to produce Spatial Durbin Models (SDM), which were used to examine the spillover effects of naloxone laws (Erfanian et al., 2019) and drug overdose mortality (Marotta et al., 2019). The final group of spatial regression specifications present in the reviewed studies are techniques relating to geographically weighted regression (GWR). GWR approaches are useful to researchers seeking to determine whether an opioid-related health measure under consideration is best modeled using global specifications or spatially non-stationary specifications (Brunsdon et al., 1998). Upcoming methods in spatial epidemiology are hierarchical modeling and Bayesian estimation techniques. The application of statistical modeling techniques to geographic units using both non-spatial regression on geographic units and spatial regression specifications contributed many analyses using GIScience. Amongst these articles, spatial methods are commonly used solely to calculate travel distance and time, except for Earnest et al. Spatial regression models such as spatial econometrics and heterogeneity models [19,20], can be used to model medical transportation while accounting for spatial dependence in the observations, thus allowing for improved estimates.

results.title: Sage Research Methods - The SAGE Handbook of Spatial Analysis - Geographically Weighted Regression
results.content: Nowhere is this more evident than in the use of what is undoubtedly the most frequently used statistical modelling approach in the analysis of spatial data – that of regression. In a typical linear regression model applied to spatial data we assume a stationary process (often without giving this any thought!). Consequently, if there is spatial nonstationarity, the resulting single parameter estimate would then represent an average of the different processes operating over space and we would only get an inkling of this through the residuals of the model. Or we might compute an autocorrelation statistic for the residuals or we might even try to ‘model’ the error dependency with various types of spatial regression models. It seems much more obvious to allow the parameter estimates in the model to vary over space rather than to calibrate a stationary model and then trying to examine a possible error in the model through the spatial patterning of the residuals.
